newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Barrage of data awaited.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Barrage of data awaited.

text.p: Bond market participants faced a full plate of meaningful economic data to digest this week -- statistics that could move prices dramatically.

Most important were the quarterly Employment Cost Index on Tuesday and monthly non-farm payrolls report on Friday. But also due were new home sales on Monday; March durable goods and April consumer confidence on Tuesday; preliminary first quarter GDP and Chicago purchasing managers on Wednesday; NAPM and personal income and consumption on Thursday and leading economic indicators on Friday.

A balanced budget accord also could emerge from Washington. Such an agreement could provide a short-term pop to the market, but the run-up would be short-lived unless terms of the deal mandated real cuts.

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan has made clear he would vote in favor of further tightening if the economy has not slowed from the torrid pace seen in the fourth and first quarters -- even if no obvious signs of growing inflation had surfaced in official statistical reports.
Thus the prime focus will be on the employment reports for signals of incipient wage inflation and continued tightness.

"It's going to be turmoil. We're likely to see a lot of volatility...we're going to have a lot of information for the markets," said David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities International Inc.
Resler doubted there would be much radically different in the data to be released -- they would continue to show a strong economy.

The most watched component of the ECI likely would be benefits cost as many analysts expected that savings seen in that area probably will begin to accelerate as many employers already had switched to HMO plans.

Resler said he guessed the Commerce Department's guess at first quarter GDP would be growth of 4.2 percent. However, he said the government's forecasts had been decidedly less accurate than private sector economists in the past.

"The actual headline print and the precise number are not going to be all that important. It's going to be a high number and will confirm that the economy grew at a rapid rate in the first quarter," Resler said.
Robert Brusca, chief economist at Nikko Securities International Inc, also expected strong numbers across the board, including ECI, GDP, payrolls and personal spending.
"It's going to be a busy week. Some may try to sell off ahead of the ECI," said Brusca. The market then may stabilize on GDP on Wednesday and attempt to do better at the end of the week.
Brusca said market participants may have already built in expectations of strong numbers into prices as evidenced by the response to the Treasury's auctions of two- and five-year notes last week.
"They made the two-year look good and kicked around the five-year," he said. Investors also like to see some bid to the market prior to refundings, Brusca added.

Late Friday the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was trading 4/32 lower at 93-21/32 to yield 7.14 percent. The 10-year was at 95-05/32 to yield 6.94 percent; the five year at 99-04/32 to 6.83 percent and the two year at 99-22/32 to yield 6.54 percent.
At the short end of the maturity spectrum, three- and six-month up two basis points at 5.17 percent and 5.40 percent, respectively. Year bills were unchanged at 5.73 percent.
